result.headline: Whole board: DQN scores 30.97 on the test (3-seed mean 30.68, spread 0.32), but the GA stays near 1 (seed 0: 1.01, all 100 test games starved), and the reward, not the 1,083 inputs alone, is the likely cause.
result.summary:
**DQN** (double DQN, a learner that predicts the value of each move from remembered games) did well. Its test mean was 30.97 apples per game (median 32, max 44), with 269 steps per game and only 9 steps per apple, so it moves efficiently. Its 65 body crashes and 35 wall crashes show it dies by hitting itself or the walls, not by wandering. Across seeds it was very consistent (30.34 to 30.97). Its training curve rose from 0.16 (start) to 13.83 by minute 2.7 and 19.4 by minute 3.6, then plateaued between about 19 and 23 for the rest of the 10 minutes. The training mean (22.5) sits below the test score because training still includes random exploration moves.

**GA** (evolution: a population of networks is scored, the best are kept and mutated) barely learned. Its seed-0 test mean was 1.01 (median 1, max 5), with 425 steps per game and 421 steps per apple. Every one of its 100 test games ended by starving, which means the snake looped without eating until the game forced it to stop. Across the three seeds the GA mean was 1.76 (values 1.01, 1.02, 3.25; spread 1.29), so the GA result is poor and noisy. Its population mean rose from 0.06 to about 0.58, but its curve was flat at 0.4 to 0.7 for most of the run. The GA ran about 39 million environment steps (game moves) in 10 minutes, roughly 65,000 steps per second, versus about 360,000 steps for DQN at roughly 600 per second.
result.diagnosis:
The reward is the main suspect for the GA. The score reward gives +10 per apple and -10 per crash, and nothing for starving. A snake that loops forever therefore scores 0, while one that crashes scores -10. Evolution finds that safe looping beats risky play, which matches the 100 of 100 starved test games. Runs in this lab that included a starvation penalty (for example the rays runs with starve 10) ended with few or no starved games. So this run cannot show that full vision hurts the GA: the reward gives the GA a loophole, and vision and reward changed together compared with lesson 04's rays run. The earlier 10-minute rays run without the survival term (same starve penalty, reward otherwise different) gave the GA 33.95 and DQN 26.75.

For DQN, the whole board looks helpful rather than harmful, even though the input vector grew 39 times. DQN learns to ignore most of the 1,083 inputs: its curve climbs fast once exploration falls (epsilon-greedy exploration reaches its final value around 100,000 steps, about minute 3), and then stays flat. Its plateau is more likely a learning limit within 10 minutes than a sign that more information is useless. Compute matters too: the full-vision DQN got only about 363,000 steps in 10 minutes, fewer than the rays run's roughly 920,000, yet it scored higher. Reward and step count differ between these runs, so treat that gap as suggestive, not proof.
result.learned: More information is not automatically better: a huge input can slow an agent (the GA here ran far fewer useful games), but a reward that accidentally rewards looping can wreck a run no matter what the snake sees. When two runs differ, check every setting, including reward and time, before blaming the one you meant to change.

recommendations.title: Compare rays depth 4 with the same reward
recommendations.why: The GA's failure may come from the reward loophole rather than the inputs. Switching back to rays depth 4 while keeping this run's score reward isolates the vision effect on both agents.
recommendations.change: Switch vision from whole board to rays with depth 4 (28 inputs), keeping the apple and death reward and the 10-minute budget.
recommendations.prediction: If the reward is the cause, the GA still starves in more than 80 of 100 test games with a mean below 3; DQN lands between 25 and 32.
recommendations.question: Is the GA's looping caused by the whole board's 1,083 inputs, or by the reward having no starvation penalty?

recommendations.title: Add a starvation penalty to whole board
recommendations.why: The score reward pays nothing for starving but -10 for crashing, so looping is the safest GA strategy. Adding a starve penalty should remove that loophole and show whether the GA can learn on the whole board.
recommendations.change: Add a starve penalty of 10 to the score reward (apple 10, death 10, starve 10), keeping full vision and the 10-minute budget.
recommendations.prediction: GA starved games fall from 100 to under 10 of 100, and the GA test mean rises above 5 from 1.01; DQN changes by less than 3 points.
recommendations.question: Does penalising starvation fix the GA's looping on the whole board?

recommendations.title: Train whole board for 40 minutes
recommendations.why: DQN's training mean plateaued from about minute 3.6 while the GA was still climbing. Four times the training time shows whether the whole board is slower to learn or simply worse.
recommendations.change: Raise the time budget from 10 to 40 minutes, keeping every other setting.
recommendations.prediction: DQN test stays within 2 points of 31 (plateau); the GA rises but stays under 5.
recommendations.question: Is the whole board just slower to learn from, or does it plateau below what rays reach?

ideas.title: Convolutional network for the whole board
ideas.what: Add a network option that reads the full-board pictures with convolutional layers, which share weights across neighbouring squares, instead of one fully connected layer over 1,083 inputs.
ideas.why: DQN ran at only about 600 steps per second on whole-board inputs and got about 363,000 steps in 10 minutes. Its plateau suggests it has to relearn that nearby squares are related. The GA also needs to mutate about 17,000 weights.
ideas.expected: Several times more steps per second and a higher DQN plateau (over 35 in 10 minutes), without the GA slowdown.

ideas.title: Warn when a comparison changes several settings
ideas.what: When two runs in a lesson differ in more than the setting under test (here reward, time and vision), show a clear diff with a warning that the comparison is confounded.
ideas.why: This run's note says only vision changed from the rays-4 run, yet its reward (score only) and time (10 minutes) differ from that run's reward (with potential and hunger) and its 5-minute budget. That confound made the GA result hard to attribute.
ideas.expected: Fewer misread comparisons: learners would see the reward or time difference before drawing a conclusion from the vision change.
